title: Principles
author: Ray Dalio
blurb: Ray Dalio founded Bridgewater Associates, which became one of the world's largest hedge funds. In Principles, he argues that success comes less from being smart than from having clear rules for handling reality. He begins with his own story, including a disastrous wrong call in 1982 that nearly wiped him out and taught him humility. From there, he lays out his life principles. Accept reality as it is. Treat painful mistakes as lessons. Follow a five-step loop from goals to results. Stay radically open-minded about your ego and blind spots. In the work section, he shows how Bridgewater built an idea meritocracy, a culture of radical truth and transparency where the best ideas win. He weighs opinions by track record and treats the organization like a machine that can be diagnosed and improved.

lessons.t: The Bet That Nearly Broke Him
lessons.b: After his confident 1982 prediction of economic collapse proved wrong and nearly ruined him, Dalio stopped asking whether he was right and started asking how he could know he was right.

(fix: Move the magnifier so its rim frames the text without crossing letters (e.g., centre the lens over the whole pill with a larger radius, or offset it to the right edge of the pill). Alternatively, layer the text above the rim.)

lessons.t: Embrace Reality and Deal With It
lessons.b: Good outcomes start with seeing the world as it really is, not as you wish it were, and then working with it.
issues: scene 8: The 'HOW IT WORKS' label on the notepad card is very small, about 16px at 1600 width, below the 18px minimum. (fix: Increase the label font size to at least 20px, enlarging the card slightly if needed so the label fits with padding.)

lessons.b: Painful mistakes are signals, and if you reflect on them honestly, they become the fastest route to growth.

lessons.t: The Five-Step Loop to Your Goals
lessons.b: Set clear goals, spot the problems in the way, diagnose their root causes, design a plan, and then push it through to results, over and over.
Your ego and your blind spots are the two biggest barriers to good decisions, and radical open-mindedness is the cure for both.
